utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. Welcome back. Mr. McCloskey, I see you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone. Yes we're ready to go. I just wanted to let you know a couple of things. We have had a status change for three documents that I think you'll want on the record, which is P2304, and that is from confidential to public; and P2337, from public to confidential; and P2298, from public to confidential. That had to do with Witness PW-057.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will look into the matter and come back to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I was -- as you know, I am about an hour and a half beyond actually what I'd estimated, and beyond what I had taken on direct with Mr. Butler in the Popovic case which is how I based my estimate, and, interestingly, Butler and I used 232 documents in the Popovic case, and I had reduced it to 190 in this case, so I think the basic explanation is we went much faster in the last case because most everyone was bilingual and represented by counsel. So we're absolutely fine with the pace, as I think everyone is, and we'll try to keep to that, but I think that's basically the reason. We may be talking more this trial but I don't think too much more. So that is the -- that's the basis of -- of the -- I think the -- the estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not too concerned about the length of the examination-in-chief. On the other hand, and it affects the whole trial, and, of course, the accused will have additional time for his cross-examination. Just one correction: You said at the beginning that you are about one hour and a half beyond your estimation. In fact, it's more than 2 hours and a half, I was told by the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. I'm an hour and a half past what I had gone in the Popovic case, and I thought it was around the same for this case, but it's even longer, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, that was my misunderstanding. The witness should be brought in, please. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish everyone good afternoon. And I would just like to ask Mr. McCloskey to explain further P2298, where he mentioned that the status of this document should be changed from public to confidential. I see that this document is a map, and I don't really understand why the status has to be changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The -- the initials of the witness are on the -- on the map, as far as I'm -- been told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We can come back to that matter later. Now we should deal with the witness, I think. Mr. Butler, welcome back to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We -- I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey is continuing his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We continue with the chronology of documents and intercepts. I will skip ahead a bit because some of the documents in the order you either already discussed or are in evidence. But let's go to 65 ter 889. That should be 141 in the -- in the tab. And as we'll see, this is an intercept synopsis that we obtained from the Croatian government, and it's dated 13th July 1995 at 1125 hours. And we can see here, I won't read it all out, it talks about Colonel Ljubisa Beara of the Main Staff, that he sent to Kasaba four buses, two trucks, one trailer-truck, for transportation of captured Muslims. Talks about sending to Batkovic. And "a selection will be made between the war criminals or just soldiers." What is your analysis of this document, of this intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, in this particular context, just operating from the summary that we have, the particular intercept operators summarised the conversation relating to Colonel Beara in orders that they believe that he has given to send vehicles to bring people to the camp at Batkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would this be consistent with what was going on, on the 13th of July? Are you aware of any evidence that on the 13th of July anyone was sent to -- any of the Muslim able-bodied men were actually sent to Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The presence of Colonel Beara and vehicles going to Kasaba to pick up Muslims is consistent. However, I'm not aware of any evidence that was produced throughout the course of the investigation that indicates that any prisoners were sent from the Srebrenica area to Batkovica that early. It is one of the issues that I am aware the investigation did look at and came up with no evidence to suggest that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer this intercept into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 889 shall be assigned exhibit number P2537. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next document, P842.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is an intercept between X and Y at 1602 hours --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This confidential document should not be broadcast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it talks about an extension down at Kasaba. X then goes on to say: "Where Malinic unit is. They said that there are 1500 gathered at the stadium." Can you remind us who you believe Malinic is and what this is a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Malinic is it Major Zoran Malinic, who is the commander of the military police battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment. The 1500 individuals that they are talking about in this context and at this time would be those captured Bosnian Muslims who were attempting to cross the road between Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba who were being captured by the VRS in that area and who were being held on the football pitch there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And to remind us of the -- P125, the document that came out under the name of Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic, in that document we'll recall that it begins by stating that there are over 1.000 members of the former 28th Division of the so-called BiH Army captured in the area of Dusanovo Kasaba. Prisoners are under the control of the military police battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment. Is this intercept consistent with that? The numbers are a little different.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, other than the numbers, the general description of the situation is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And P125 has a date delivered -- or excuse me, a time delivered at 1510 hours. This is 1602 hours. Would an increase from over 1.000 to 1500, would that be consistent with the events as you learned of them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The investigation has detailed that prisoners were being captured all through the day and, in fact, even through the subsequent days. Although there are no known survivors on -- after the 13th that I'm aware. So the fact that the numbers would be increasing is certainly consistent with what I understand is happening in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's now go to P413A. And I -- you've discussed this already in your earlier testimony so I won't go along, I won't go into detail. But we just note here that a few lines down the page, it says: "At each point there are roughly 1500 to 2.000." And this intercept is at 1730 hours today. Is that consistent or inconsistent with the previous document, two documents you just spoke of?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's consistent, sir. They're all related.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document, P1570A, which is an intercept. And can you relate this intercept to any other intercept that you have already spoken about? If you recall.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe late last week, Thursday, I discussed an intercept between General Krstic and Ljubisa Borovcanin that occurred at roughly 2030 hours on 13 July 1995. Here, at 1945 hours, prior to that, this is a particular intercept where a correspondent is calling from General Krstic looking for Ljubisa and, of course, the phrase "who has gone to Bratunac." And they're talking about one bus from Janja and other parts of the Janja Detachment which -- in Doboj which leads me again to the conclusion that Ljubisa in this context is Ljubisa Borovcanin because these are all locations where MUP forces are coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is this consistent or inconsistent with the -- a conversation between Borovcanin and Krstic that you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this dove-tails right into that. This is General Krstic saying he wants to talk to Borovcanin and roughly 45 minutes later, Borovcanin calls back, you know, as requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At 1945 hours where do you believe General Krstic was located?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was located in Vlasenica, given the fact that, at approximately 2000 hours, he is given command of the Drina Corps there by General Mladic. So 15 minutes prior to when that ceremony or event occurs he is at the Drina Corps hours in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to P1601, which is from the Drina Corps command, 13 July. It's the regular combat report to the Main Staff. We see in the situation of the zone of responsibility notation that in Konjevic Polje and also in Nova Kasaba reception of Muslim civilians and soldiers whose surrender is being carried out, taken in an organised fashion. What -- can you relate this comment to anything you've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular comment refers to the thousands of Bosnian Muslim men, able-bodied men, who are being detained -- captured and then detained at various locations; Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje and further towards Bratunac, on 13 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We don't see a reference to prisoners detained at Kravica or the nearby Sandici field. Do you see any reference about that in there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And by 1945 hours, had the Kravica warehouse massacre already been going on for some time? I think you've testified about that recently.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. My understanding is that the massacre began at approximately 1700 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we can go to page 3 in the English. And it's the -- it should be the next page -- sorry, page 3 in the B/C/S as well. And we can see a document signed and -- under the name of Commander Major-General Radislav Krstic. And we see that some unit - I can't tell from the stamp - had received this document at 1945 hours. How does this part of this document fit into your evaluation about where Krstic was and whether or not he was commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, it's consistent in so much as we know that on the 13th July at approximately 2000 hours he went from being the Chief of Staff to the commander of the Drina Corps, so the signature block is functionally correct as it should be if he were the commander. Whomever received this document, whether it's the Drina Corps com centre or it's for another unit, 15 or 20 minutes earlier from where I would believe, or at least where I understand that the change of command took place at 2000, so I don't see it as generally inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's go to P1562.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is confidential and should not be broadcast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see here, we have an intercept, between Deronjic and X, who is described as Karadzic's intermediary. And it says in parentheses that that intermediary and Karadzic are sitting in the same room. Who do you believe this Deronjic is in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the investigation has established that this is Miroslav Deronjic, who, at this time, is President Karadzic's designated civilian commissioner for the Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And as far as you know, has this intermediary ever been identified?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So the intermediary says: "I'm waiting for a call to President Karadzic. Is he there?" And B says: "Yes." Which, let me go back to the beginning, that it says Badem. Can you remind us what you believe Badem means, what this B would be? Or, sorry, what is Badem?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Badem is the telephonic code-name for the Bratunac Brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where in your analysis do you think Deronjic is when he is speaking on this conversation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would be at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Basically it says: Badem says: "Hello. I have Deronjic on the line." The intermediary, known as X, says: "Deronjic, speak up." Deronjic says: "Hello, yes. I can hear you." And X, the intermediary says: "Deronjic, the president is asking how many thousands." What do you think in this context the president is asking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that numbered thousands at that juncture would be the numbers of Bosnian Muslim men being detained on 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And by 8.10, 2010 hours, can you remind us, were there men actually staying in Bratunac town?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. By that time, men had been placed in an old hangar facility. They were in the Vuk Karadzic school and in a number of buses and trucks, parked in front of other facilities to include Vuk Karadzic because there was no more room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then Deronjic says, in response to how many thousands, Deronjic says: "About 2 for the time being." Is 2.000 men consistent or in consistent with your knowledge of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the number of prisoners taken, or at least being described as taken, it would probably be a little low. One of the factors is that there were a group of men - I'm not sure of the number - who were also held in vehicles in and around the village of Kravica. So like I said, I think 2.000 is a bit low for who was in Bratunac that evening. Plus, also taking into account that at around that same time, the first buses and trucks were going from Bratunac to facilities in the Zvornik Brigade zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then it is goes on to say the intermediary says: "Two, Mr. President." Then "(heard in the background)." Deronjic says: "But there will be more during the night." Where would more -- if they're talking about prisoners, where would the more be coming from, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those would be prisoners detained in some of the more outlying locations from Bratunac, which would includes Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then Deronjic says: "Do want me to come done there to Cerska?" What do you make of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigation has determined that Cerska is the location or nickname that President Karadzic's offices were in the Pale area, so, in this context, Deronjic is asking, if you want me to travel to that location to personally brief you on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then X the intermediary says: "It's best that you send it by telegram." Deronjic says: "Can you hear me, President?" The intermediary X says: "The President can't hear you, Deronjic. "This is the intermediary." Deronjic says: "I have about 2.000 here by now and then ..." with a note that the teleprinter drowns him out. If Deronjic was speaking in the Bratunac Brigade coms room, would that be consistent with a teleprinter being in the same room, if have you any idea?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One would think so, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now the intermediary says: "Deronjic, the president says: All the goods must be placed inside the warehouses before 12.00 tomorrow." Deronjic says: "Right." And then, X, the intermediary says: "Deronjic, not in warehouses, but somewhere else. Understood?" What is your analysis of those few lines, all the goods -- the president says: "All the goods must be placed inside the warehouses before 12.00 tomorrow"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular context, the people speaking to Deronjic appear to have some awareness that sometime after noon on 1400 or after noon on the 14th of July, I should say, that some observers would potentially coming through Bratunac, and there was a concern that whoever those individuals would be, they did not want any outside observers seeing the Muslim prisoners in facilities in Bratunac. So, again, an order to place them in other facilities and other locations where they cannot be observed by whomever -- you know, the people representing Karadzic are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So by 12.00, let's -- on the 14th, where were the thousands of Bosnian Muslims that had been in Bratunac on the 13th, or in that area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: By 12.00 on the 14th, the final groups of those prisoners from Bratunac who were in the Orahovac facility at Grabovica were in that gym. At the same time, they were still moving people in the Petkovci, the old -- the school at Petkovci, and also further north in the facility at Rocevic. However, given the sheer number of people who were being captured and stored in that location, they were still moving people out of Bratunac all through the day on the 14th. And perhaps even as early as the early morning hours of the 15th. Some of the last people to arrive in the Pilica area and subsequently there was no room at the school in Pilica and they were actually put in the Pilica dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to next to the next one, 65 ter 2984, an intercept which the case will show is from 14 July, 2227 hours. That should be 2984A. Thank you. And I don't want to get into a lot of detail on this, but this shows a General Vilotic and a Jokic, the Palma duty officer. Can you remind us what Palma is and who you think this Jokic is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Palma is the telephonic code-name for the Zvornik Infantry Brigade headquarters, and on the 14th of July, 1995, the duty officer of the brigade was Major Dragan Jokic, who was also the chief of engineering for the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you heard of a General Vilotic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I believe, in this particular context, the correspondent is in fact General Miletic from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How is it you come up with that opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When -- well, first, I'm not aware of any other general officer named Vilotic in the VRS. And, clearly, the context of this conversation, where it was intercepted and what they're talking about, is off of the army of the Republika Srpska radio telephone network. We did actually even go as far as investigatively of trying to determine if at the same time there was potentially a General Vilotic with the federal republic of Yugoslav army, just to ensure that it wasn't a call coming in from perhaps Belgrade or something of that nature, and the investigation, it failed to turn up anyone named General Vilotic in that particular aspect. So given my own knowledge of the communications systems, how it is, you know, occasionally garbled, I believe in this context the operator mistook the name Vilotic and instead it's Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And looking at that first line it says: "Where is Obradovic?" And P says: "In the field." And then as you look down we see references to the chief and where the chief is. What is your opinion -- and we later on see that Jokic says: "Obrenovic is really engaged to the hilt." So what's your view on this first: "Where is Obradovic?" Who do you think that is? Do you know of an Obradovic in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. And, again, you know, I believe that the intercept operators mistook the name Obrenovic for Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2984A shall be assigned exhibit number P2538. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we go to P18. And it's page 14 in the English, and it's dated -- it's for the dates 14 and 15 July of the B/C/S, I'm sorry, I don't have a page. But if you flip through it, you will see it goes by dates. So if we could just go to 14 in English and ... Yes, that's the -- that's the English. And the -- the Serbian should have a marking pretty clearly. Yes, right on the money. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you can recall, I didn't stay on the front page very long, what this is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular document is a log-book that was from the Zvornik -- I'm sorry, the Bratunac military police platoon, and it is their daily log-book where they note where all of the officers are on any particular day and what activity that they are engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this reference that we see: "The police was engaged in the escort of Muslim refugees." What is your opinion on who the police were and who these Muslim refugees were?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The police were the Bratunac Brigade Military Police Platoon. On the 14th and 15th, there were no civilians to my knowledge being escorted out of Bratunac. They'd all been removed by the evening of 13 July, and when I use the phrase "civilians" in this context it's the women, children, and elderly from Potocari. The only people being moved on the 14th and 15th of July are the military-aged men who had been previously detained from Potocari, or who had been captured elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to -- now to P124. Now, this is a document from the command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade. Remind us the town associated with that command post?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this would be Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's dated 14 July, and it's sector for intelligence and security. Drina Corps Command. Drina Corps IKM, personally to Krstic. Command of the 65th Projection Regiment. Entitled: "Situation in Zepa." And from the second -- well, from the first page of the Serbian we can see it's in the name of General Tolimir. It's also noted in the English. And what I want to ask you about is on page 2 of the English, in the middle of the page, it says: "Early this morning, since 0500 hours, in the area of responsibility of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade and above the Muslim enclaves of Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde there is an unmanned aerial vehicle whose flight path we can determine only by sound. "It is probably recording the positions and ... movements of units. Radio communication interference is registered. The orders for camouflage measures and organisation of multiple communications systems -- system have been issued." And then it goes on. So can you -- just give us initially how would General Tolimir have come into this information? Just generally, if you don't know specifically.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tracking of these types of threats would be an event that would be reported up through the various command posts. If General Tolimir is present at the -- one of the command posts, either the main or forward command post of the Rogatica Brigade, he is going to be in a position to hear these reports come in, evaluate their significance, and turn around and issue his own orders as a result of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From what you know from the investigation, were unmanned aircraft used by any forces in Bosnia around this time-frame?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The NATO forces did have access to several UAV platforms that were operating in and around Eastern Bosnia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, again, from your knowledge of the investigation, what is a UAV platform?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: UAV simply stands for unmanned aerial vehicle. It is a remotely controlled pilotless aircraft. Generally its primary function, particularly back at this time-frame, was to provide aerial reconnaissance of ground targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And General Tolimir is reporting that, among other places, this craft is flying above the enclave of Srebrenica. If General Tolimir is down in the Rogatica, Zepa, Borike area on the 14th, how is it or why is it in your view he would be concerned receiving information from the Srebrenica area and then passing on information from the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are two parts to the question, I guess. The first part is he would be -- you know, with respect to his receiving the information, command is -- in his integrated system, he is going to be in a position, just like all of the other units are in this respect, to receive the reports from various units. They're all within the Drina Corps. So his ability to monitor that, even though he is dealing with Zepa and the situations around Srebrenica, is -- is perfectly consistent with what the communications would allow. I mean, that's not a problem. The second part of your question, why would he be concerned, is because at this time this remains, still, an integrated operation. The military forces that are going to be taking place and dealing with Zepa, many of them are coming from or just recently arrived from Srebrenica. So, as a professional intelligence officer in this context, he is going to understand that it's more than just what I have in front of me here at Zepa with respect to being concerned about what information the enemy can gain. What information the enemy can glean over the Srebrenica enclave with respect to where military units are or are not located, would give whoever is doing that observation indications on where they might be in other locations, such as Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall from the investigation any activity that was going on on the ground around the village of Glogova and the Kravica warehouse on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Beginning the morning of the 14th of July, there were -- or, actually, late evening, the 13th, if I recall correctly, but certainly during the day of the 14th, they were removing bodies from the Kravica warehouse, and they were being brought to the Glogova location where a mass grave had been dug, and the bodies from Kravica were being placed in the mass grave in Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would you say that receiving this information and then reporting it out to the people addressed here would be part of General Tolimir's position as assistant commander for intelligence and security?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what -- what part of his -- his job, what label, if any, this activity that he is doing and reporting on would fit under his job?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be something that would fall on the security side, given the context of trying to deny friendly information or information about VRS military forces and the situation on the ground to potentially hostile intelligence sources, which, given the UAV context, would be NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document, which is P00128. We see it's the -- from the same place. Dated 14 July to the Drina Corps Command from General Tolimir. And handwritten it's 1045 hours. I won't repeat it all, but it basically appears to be talking about an unmanned aerial vehicle reconnoitring the area and jamming the radio communications. Do you relate this document to the previous document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is -- it's a supplemental report directly to the Drina Corps on the same situation, essentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it talks about it a bit in the paragraphs, and then in the final paragraph, it says: "If spotted, the unmanned aerial vehicle must be destroyed immediately." How do you take that as -- as -- that statement? Is that a proposal, an order, a request? What is that in your view, militarily?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be an order, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that kind of an order consistent with his job as assistant commander for security and intel that's working out of the Zepa area at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not strictly consistent, but it again reflects his knowledge of the broader plan, as well as the guidance that has been given to the Drina Corps air defence forces relating to these types of situations. Again, in the context that I read this, General Tolimir is not going to give an order or a direction that he believes he's not authorised to give.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to P129. This is another document from Rogatica Brigade, 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade. 14 July. To several addressees that I won't repeat. And if we see on the bottom of the Serbian, it's -- it's, again, from General Tolimir. It is entitled: "Placing the UNPROFOR check-points under control." And could we go to page 2 of the English. Just leading up to page 2 it says: "For the time being, we have taken full control over the check-point number 2 at Boksanica where the command of the UNPROFOR forces is located. We have wire connection with it. The check-point will remain functioning as it is not blocked -- as if it is not blocked and surrounded by our forces. We plan to direct the work of the other UN check-points through this check-point. We have instructed the UNPROFOR command to issue instructions to their check-points not to open fire on VRS units and instead -- and to instead simulate the action by shooting in the air if forced to do so by the Muslims." What's going on here, in your view, that General Tolimir is reporting on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At some juncture of time, the VRS had approached the Ukrainian Detachment related to Zepa and had effectively co-opted them to assist the VRS by providing information and not resisting VRS military moves into the Zepa enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know clearly one way or another whether this co-option you're talking about was by force or by plan or some other means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that. No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to P480. Another Rogatica Brigade document from the 14th. In the name of General Tolimir. Personally to General Miletic. Is this the same Miletic you were talk being earlier in your discussion about Vilotic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it is entitled: "Protection of Secret Military Information," known as TVP. And in here, we see that General Tolimir is saying it's necessary to incorporate the Main Staff of the VRS in the work-plan of the Drina Corps. And he is talking, I won't repeat it all, about getting these radios. Can you explain why General Tolimir in his position, if he is in the Rogatica area, would be dealing with this subject matter?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir is seeking to effectively align the Main Staff, at least their knowledge of what the Drina Corps is doing, as well as the subordinate brigades related to Zepa, and wants to be able to monitor the Drina Corps communications network that was established for the Zepa operation. Clearly he doesn't have the appropriate equipment to do that. One would think that as a general he can just tell the Rogatica Brigade to give up their equipment. In fact, he can't. The brigade commander needs that particular equipment in order to effectively command his brigade. He doesn't have the right to just take that type of equipment away from him. So his obvious logical process here is that he is going to go back to his headquarters, the Main Staff, and request that they send down the appropriate equipment so he has his own set to be able to listen to these communications functions. It is, again, as I've said before, a process of integrated command. General Tolimir, for him to give effective orders as to what is going on and what actions need to take place from his perspective on the Main Staff, needs to have a detailed knowledge of what subordinate formations are doing, what they're involved in, and what orders they've received. Otherwise, the risk again is that General Tolimir is giving orders that are contrary to -- or -- or, actually, will damage the situation on the ground because he doesn't have a complete and accurate picture of what needs to happen. So this is all part of, you know, a completely integrated command and control system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your view, would he need to know about what his subordinates, Beara and Jankovic and other security officers, are doing up in the Zvornik and Bratunac area at the same time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just briefly, why?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: First off, he is still responsible for them and their activities. He is their direct superior. Second, they are carrying out the commander's orders [realtime transcript read in error "offices"], and, in fact, so is he. So for him to effectively do that, to know what orders to issue, and perhaps as importantly, what orders not to issue, he has to be aware of what the plan is, as well as what other people's roles in the plan are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you've concluded that let's say Beara, Jankovic, Popovic are carrying out the commander's, Mladic's orders, but how can you conclude that he is? How do you know he is not just dealing with Zepa and hiding or ignoring the murders that are going on, on the 14th, 15th, and 16th of July by his -- under the organisation of his people, Beara, Jankovic and others?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May God's peace reign in this house and may God's will be done in these proceedings. Could Mr. McCloskey give us the exact reference, showing what it is that I'm hiding or covering up when he talks about murders and killings. Or perhaps he could tell us that all these things are just his assumptions, his evaluations, and his opinions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you get the floor, Mr. McCloskey, in page 22, line 16, I read, I: "Second, they are carrying out the commander's officers, and so in fact so is he." Just going to disappear from the screen. Were you really, sir, talking about the commander's officers, or what was your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, that should be the "commander's orders."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question was not that General Tolimir was hiding. My question was: How do you know when you say General Tolimir is following the commander's orders that he was not just ignoring those orders or not doing anything, or -- and in fact, hiding from them. How do you know that. Why do you conclude he is following the commander's orders, how do you know he wasn't avoiding them or ignoring them. That was the question. I don't mean to suggest General Tolimir is hiding. That may have been a bad choice of words. More ignoring or avoiding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Mr. Butler, are you able to respond?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As I discussed earlier, I believe it was last week, the underlying foundation, when I look at the roles and activities of various individuals, is on the basis of the fact that, as professional military officers - and in the context of all of the people that we're discussing they are - they're going to perform their duties in an efficient and diligent manner. As I also said, even in the context of an unlawful act, like the massacre of thousands of prisoners, being that it was a military organisation that they were going to do so in the military manner in which they had been trained. And, in fact, the information that has been developed through the years of investigation substantiates that, to a large degree, all of the military processes related to collecting the prisoners, transporting the prisoners, moving the prisoner, the execution of the prisoners, the resources needed for that, the burial of the prisoners, and even the reburial of the prisoners, was accomplished in a large degree by soldiers and officers, many of whom are actually cataloguing their participation in various aspects of this broader massacre, because fuel and ammunition and other things had to be accounted for. So when the situation occurs as the question has come up from Mr. McCloskey, how would I conclude that, I look at it from the perspective of General Tolimir's role within the army and the diligent and responsible function of his duties. The fact that his subordinates are heavily engaged in this particular criminal aspect dealing with Srebrenica, they're doing so in a synchronised manner and that General Tolimir's responsibility as their first immediate superior is to know what they're doing and what orders that they are carrying out. It would be a completely irregular situation to have, where a particular officer's subordinates are engaged in activities, military or unlawful, on the basis of an order from somebody else and that the officer who directly supervises their activities and directs their activities, then-General Tolimir would be ignorant of that situation. The last part of Mr. McCloskey's question, the wilful ignorance issue, I guess in the abstract it would be possible that even though all of the mechanisms for command existed and that as noted by the volume of information that I've discussed so far relating to who was talking to who about what, you know, it is conceivable in the abstract that General Tolimir could have elected to remain wilfully ignorant of what was going on for whatever reason. Other individuals who have been before previous Trial Chamber have made the same argument. That, of course, becomes an area outside of my particular expertise. It's just all I can say about that, is that, he obviously had all of the necessary communications means to be informed as to what was going on, why it was going, and whose orders. And if he were diligently exercising his responsibilities as the assistant commander for intelligence and security on the Main Staff, I guess I would find it staggering, frankly, that he wouldn't know and have no idea of the scope and scale of the massacres that were occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's the point of knowledge. Can you remind us what his responsibility would be, if any, regarding the -- once he is -- knows that his subordinate, Beara, Jankovic, and others are carrying out this material, what would his responsibility be in monitoring, working with, overseeing, directing these people in their tasks, if any?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. These are -- this is just speculation. Could Mr. McCloskey please give a reference as to where he finds that General Tolimir knew of these events and what he was describing as his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can provide him a short outline. If you'd like. It's evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, if you look at the transcript, Mr. McCloskey decided to use another formulation. He said: "Can you remind us what his responsibility would be, if any, regarding -- the" and then he reformulated, "... knows that the subordinate, Beara, Jankovic, and others are carrying out this material, what his responsibility be in monitoring," and so on. This is slightly different wording of the question. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes Mr. President. This is, of course, as you've pointed out in the form of a hypothetical. And it's up to the Court to determine the issues, as Mr. Butler is -- has I think just said. So the best way to ask this question, in my view, is the way I did it. Hypothetically, if the General knows about his subordinates doing these things, what would be his normal duties and responsibilities regarding them and their work. It's a hypothetical and not a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can you answer that hypothetical?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I guess in two different scenarios. It would depend on what his normal duty in that sense would be. If he were conducting his duty completely within the framework of his responsibilities as the assistant commander of intelligence and security, and in accordance with the laws of the Republika Srpska and the relevant regulations on the application of the laws of war within the army, then once he were to receive knowledge that his subordinates were participating in this crime he would have duties to have them arrested, presumably, or, otherwise, relieved from that their posts and undertake an investigation because law enforcement in that context is a function of the intelligence and security branch. It's the military police. If normal is to facilitate the commander's orders, then his knowledge of what his subordinates were doing would be important. So again he knew what orders he might need to give in order to facilitate that work, as well as what orders not to give so it did not interfere. So in this particular situation, I mean, he -- he has two hypothetical tracks that he could go down. One hypothetical track is based on gaining knowledge of the crimes that are occurring and doing his duty within the context of the laws and regulations; and the other one is the hypothetical track of finding out about the crimes and doing his duty to fully implement his commander's orders and to make his subordinates available, as required, and to give any other orders necessary in order to ensure they complete their work in the most effective and efficient means possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if - again, with a hypothetical - if General Tolimir becomes aware that his subordinates are involved in criminal conduct and allows them to continue in that criminal conduct, is he in fact making his people available to Mladic, as you've said?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- not only as I've said in this context, but as outlined in the SFRY regulations on the laws of war and their applicability. It talks about the situation where, as a superior officer, you gain knowledge of a war crime occurring and if you fail to take measures to prevent it or to mitigate the damages from it, if you have the ability to do so, you incur at least in that context a legal responsibility for the actions. That's not inconsistent with most other aspects of command. When a commander or superior recognises his subordinates are engaged in any activity, if he fails to stop that activity, not even supposing it's unlawful or not I mean, but not giving any orders to those particular subordinates, the subordinates are free to interpret that the actions that they are involved in, they are doing in compliance with the wishes of the superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: All right. I just wanted an explanation. Just now you have stated that: "When a commander or superior recognises his subordinates are engaged in any activity, if he fails to stop that activity, not even supposing it's unlawful, or not, I mean, but not giving any orders to those particular subordinate, the subordinates are free to interpret that the actions that they are involved in, they are doing in," I suppose, "in compliance with the wishes of the superior." Does that apply even to an activity that is unlawful, which they must know as subordinates that it is unlawful. Are they entitled to assume that it is okay for them to do that with the wishes of the superior? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under the SFRY, later adopted the RS law, legally you're correct. They are not permitted to assume that. In a practical sense of command, however, what happens frequently is that subordinates will often take their queues from a superior. One particular hypothetical situation might be that a group of soldiers would take a prisoner and shoot that particular prisoner. They would then look down the road, be aware that their commander has witnessed that act. The question is what happens next. If the commander takes immediate action, the lesson that the subordinates draw is that that type of conduct will not be condoned. If the officer, once he becomes aware of that act, turns and walks away, the practical reality for the subordinates is that they understand that that type of behaviour will be condoned by the command and that they're free to continue on to do it without fear of retribution. So I do take your point, ma'am. Obviously there is a legal responsibility not to engage in this. But certainly, from a practical command point, soldiers might not -- at the lower levels certainly might not have that same appreciation as officers should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, it's time for the last question before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, just one more document quickly I think we can get to quickly. It's 65 ter 2204.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a document, this time under the name of General Mladic, dated 14 July. And it -- it speaks about the request of the Dutch Battalion to move out of the area. Mr. Butler, is this roughly consistent with what you know eventually occurred; DutchBat leaving the area under the authority of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer this into evidence, Mr. President, and then a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2204 shall be assigned exhibit number P2539. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We must have the first break now, and we will resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would like to now go out of order slightly and go back to P1459. This is the duty officer notebook of the Zvornik Brigade. Mr. Butler it will be up on the screen, only I -- given some of what you were just saying I want to go through a few of the days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where can we find it in the binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's a couple of pages here and there, Mr. President, but -- so I would say it's not in the binder, because I'm just going to decide if I'm -- to keep it all together, I'm going to try to keep it with the related subject matter. So if we could start at page 41 in the English. It should be 40 in the B/C/S. And it's the Prosecution's position, as you will see from this so-called teacher's edition, that this is the 14th of July. We need to get the B/C/S which should be able to be up at the same time. Oh, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what I want to you ask about Mr. Butler is this bottom section, 14 July. Prosecution's position is that it's -- Dragan Jokic is the duty officer on the 14th of July, and you've just testified about that. Do you stay with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It is my understanding that he is the duty officer on the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this reference, "Colonel Salapura called, Drago and Beara are to report to Golic." And can you briefly tell us who you think these people, what unit they belong to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Salapura is a subordinate of General Tolimir. He is the chief of the intelligence administration. Drago, in this case, I believe it's Drago Nikolic, the security officer for the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. And Beara, again, is a direct subordinate of General Tolimir. He is the chief of the security administration. Golic is Major Pavle Golic who is an intelligence officer with the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us from your review, for several years here, is Salapura a name, a common name? Do you see any other Salapuras involved in these events in any way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer if it is a common name in Serbian naming context. But with respect to the VRS, I'm only aware of one Colonel Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now let's go to page 45 in the English, and page 44. I won't ask you what's going on on the 14th in the Zvornik area. That's part of the record. Here we see, if we're still on the 14th, and at 1500 hours it says: "Colonel Beara is coming in order to Orahovac, Petkovci, Rocevic, Pilica." Is that -- that Colonel Beara, who is he, in your view here, in this context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same officer we previously discussed, the chief the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what do you take this to be a reference to, what I just read?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the locations are all - Orahovac, Petkovci, Rocevic, Pilica - are all known schools where prisoners were detained prior to their execution, this is -- Colonel Beara is coming in the Zvornik Brigade area with the intent of either visiting or dealing with the issues related to those locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now let's go to page 55 in the English, 54 in the B/C/S. We're still on 14 July. This reference, Beara to call 155. What do you make of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware from the investigation that 155 is the main phone number at the Main Staff, Panorama. So in this particular context, Beara is calling 155, or calling the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, tell us how this would work. We see this again, it's Dragan Jokic. So if this is a note from Dragan Jokic, what can we glean from how Jokic ended up writing this, if anything?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, one of the functions of the duty officer, because he's performing his duty in the duty operations centre, and because that has to be by the phone, for his -- you know, for his tour -- duty officer, he is usually the person that all incoming and outgoing issues for the unit go through. In this context, either Dragan Jokic personally or the assistant whose helping him during the performance of his duty is taking phone messages or other orders that have come in from outside the brigade, it's customary that they write them down so they don't forget them and pass them on. The military switchboard only goes as far as with respect to the radio telephone to the Zvornik headquarters. If a call or if an order comes in for not only Beara but any other officer who is around there, they're going to have find an alternate means to get the word to him. So again they're -- that's why they write things down so these issues aren't forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next page, number 57. In English, 56. And we see written in large letters on the left-hand side in the Serbian. We still need the Serbian. Thank you. Dragan Jokic is still noted as the duty officer. And it says: "From Beara, Drago to report, Mane Djukici [phoen]." And then it is says in very large print: "0900 Beara is coming." Who do you think these folks are?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beara is the same officer we discussed, Colonel Ljubisa Beara. Drago, Drago Nikolic. I -- there are a -- Mane is, I know, a very common name, so I don't want to speculate on that particular one. And, of course, the notation at 0900 Beara is coming, given the context of this is the third or fourth page of the 14th of July, I'm reading this to assume that this is a notation that Beara is coming tomorrow, in that context, the 15th of July, at 0900 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 74 in the B/C/S, and I hope 75 in the English. It's ERN 761 in the English, the last -- yes, that's correct in the English. We see at the top of the page: "Drago and Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic are to report to Major Golic early in the morning?" Are these the same people that you've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And looking down the page, we see under requests - and we know it's the position of the Prosecution that this is Drago Nikolic as duty officer - for the 1st Battalion, can you tell us, we see 50 litres of oil for transport of troops to Kula. Do you know where Kula is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's the actual village that the school is located -- we call it the Pilica school. It's actually physically located in the village of Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And also 20 litres of gasoline. Has the investigation revealed any -- any troops around that school where Muslims were held?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I am aware that members of, in part, the 1st Battalion were at that location guarding the prisoners around the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now let's go to 85 in English. 84 in the B/C/S. We're now on -- clearly on 16 July. That last communication notation -- oh, I'm sorry. Can we go to page 79 in the English and page 78 in the B/C/S. And we see that Milorad Trbic is the duty officer. Can you remind us who he is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milorad Trbic is the assistant chief of security. He worked for Drago Nikolic in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see this entry: "0855 Golic asked Popovic to call him." And who do you think that is, Golic and Popovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Golic from the Drina Corps; and Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic from the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why do you say that, as I think Golic and Popovic are relatively common names?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my context of trying to identify through the years all of the officers and all of the individuals involved in the crimes, we do run into these. I mean, I obviously hold open the possibility that there are dozens, if not hundreds, of soldiers from the Drina Corps with the last name of Popovic. The issue then becomes, given the context of what we're talking about, as well as, you know, the rank of the individuals -- I mean, the reality is that all of those other Popovics aren't going to have access to military telephones and wouldn't be calling the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. So the most logical people to presume these conversations are involved with are going to be the officers who are directing the issues related to the Drina Corps. Again, whether they're lawful or not. So that's why I take this as Major Golic and Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic calling the duty officer, as opposed to Private Golic and Private Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So as this note says Golic -- we can glean from the note that Golic has called and said, and I quote: "That he can forget what he asked for and what he wrote about. He knows what he is supposed to do according to the agreed procedure ..." Do you know the specifics of what they're talking about? For example, do you know what he wrote about, that Golic is now saying he can forget about what he wrote about? Do you have any idea what it was that Popovic wrote about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I recall or I ever knew what Popovic might have written back on 15 July. I don't know if I've ever seen an order from Popovic in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this comment: "He knows what he's supposed to do according to the agreed procedure. Boss, from Panorama, 01." What is this boss, remind us what Panorama 01 would be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Panorama is the telephonic code-name for the Main Staff. What officers would frequently do in order to give a clue to the people who they were talking to on the phone who was actually the person giving the order or something of that nature, was that if they wanted it -- people to understand that it was from the commander, it would be 01. So if you have a call from the Zvornik Brigade in -- you know, you want to talk to Zlatar -- or, I'm sorry, you want to talk to Palma 01, everyone understands that you're looking for the brigade commander. Panorama 01 [Realtime transcript read in error "Palma"] is the commander of the Main Staff, which would be General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this agreed procedure glossed from -- agreed procedure from General Mladic, what procedure would Golic, Popovic, Mladic have to do with on the 16 July, in your view? If any.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one extrapolates the conversations and the issues that we talked about previously on the 17th and the 18th, the particular intercept where the two correspondents are talking about what the procedure was and in detail what happens to those males who are between the 16 to 60 military age group, this is another reference to the agreed procedure. The fact that the boss is giving directly these orders, if one goes back in time to intercepts that occur on the 15th, Colonel Beara makes it clear in his discussions with General Zivanovic and shortly thereafter, General Krstic, about these -- you know, the orders coming from the boss personally on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler you spoke about the extension of the commander. Could you please repeat the code-name of this extension.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is -- the suffix that they use is 01. So, for example, if you're talking about over these radio telephones what the normal military discussion was, was if you wanted to talk to the brigade commander of the Zvornik Brigade, you would want to speak to Palma 01, and it was generally understood that that was the commander. Zlatar 01 is the commander of the Drina Corps. Panorama 01 is generally understood by everyone to be the commander of the Main Staff. It is just a military slang terminology people would use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand. Palma 01 is referring to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Palma in this case is the telephonic code-name of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I ask this question only because of the record. On page 37, line 12, which has just disappeared from the screen, you are recorded to having said if you want to talk to Palma 01, everyone understands that the Main Staff, which would be General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Somehow that didn't get transcribed correctly or I misspoke. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, you didn't misspeak. You said Panorama 01, I think. I just wanted to correct the transcript. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we also see that this message referred to above conveyed to Popovic at 0910. And the bottom of the page: "Beara to call Panorama 155 at 0930 hours." You've mentioned the Main Staff switchboard 155 in your view. Where in particular, or who was picking up on that line, as far as you knew, during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is the 155 line rings in the operation centre of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall who you see on intercepts or on other documents that are speaking from the Main Staff? Any high-ranking officers on these days?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most logical person who would be the senior-ranking officer there would be General Miletic, the chief of operations for the Main Staff. Other generals would be in and out of there, but that's General Miletic's primary duty position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or duty location, would probably be a better description of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to page 85 in English in the same document. We're still on 16 July. 84, B/C/S. Trbic is still the duty officer. And it says: "At 1400 hours, Popovic requested a bus with a fuel [sic] tank and 500 litres D2. Zlatar duty officer and Golic informed." What does your analysis bear, if anything, about Popovic requesting a bus with a fuel tank and 500 litres of D2. First of all, tell us what D2 is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: D2 is diesel fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how do you interpret this line?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, don't have to interpret it much, in so much as there is actually significant corroborating documentation as well as intercepts, which discusses an entire episode of Colonel Popovic requesting fuel related to the job that he had to do and that there was an entire process that went on related to what procedures had to be followed so that the fuel could be appropriately signed over to Colonel Popovic, could be brought out to him, the fuel would be consumed, and then he'd sign for the remainder of the fuel that went back. There are intercepts which talk about that process to various members of the Drina Corps rear services staff, as well as documents from the Zvornik Brigade, from their rear service, which reflect the actual withdrawal or disbursement of the fuel and the various officers who had to sign off on that. I think, as I discussed earlier, in this particular context, the use of the fuel and for what -- we're aware it was being used with, is obviously unlawful connected to the mass execution and burial thereafter, but the process is occurring along the same military manner that it would be if it were fuel going for any other variety of reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll get to the documents and intercepts you mention as we go through the chronology. But do you recall the location that this fuel was taken to to be used by Popovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what, in your opinion, was this fuel being used for by Popovic at Pilica on 16 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that they needed it for the buses that were taking people from the school at Pilica and taking them to the location in which they were executed in Branjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then this other line underneath that is: "Zlatar duty officer and Golic informed." We again hear from Golic. Which Golic do you think that is in this context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Golic from the Drina Corps, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the Zlatar duty officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, on 16 July, if I recall correctly, the Zlatar duty officer is Colonel Cerovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll check. I think there's a document related to that to see if that's true.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be Cerovic, with a C, for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. That was just the -- I wanted to get us back to the work being done by some of the people involved here. And so now if we could go back to the chronology, and I thank everyone for bearing with me, could we go to P373B. And we now see, we're on the -- we're on the 14th July. We have an intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Shouldn't be broadcast. Before we go to this, could we go to 65 ter 111.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'm not sure it's in the binders. I couldn't find it, but it will come up on the screen. It was on the list, though. I may have skipped over it by accident. Now, Mr. Butler, if you could take a look at this noting it's from the Drina Corps on the 13th July, received by someone at 20 hours -- or 2000 hours. What is this, and how does it fit into your analysis, briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As an important component obviously of the military aspect of command, everybody in all of the relevant military units has to be made aware when there is a significant change in command of a military formation. Everyone has to be on the same sheet of paper as to who the commander is. This is a particular document signed by Lieutenant-Colonel Jovicic to -- from the Drina Corps Command to all of the relevant units of the Drina Corps informing them that General Zivanovic has been relieved of command of the Drina Corps and is being reassigned to new duties, that General Krstic is assuming the post as corps commander, and that, to replace him, Colonel Svetozar Andric, who at that time is the commander of the 1st Birac Brigade, is now taking General Krstic's place as the corps Chief of Staff. So this is the formal notification so all of the subordinate formations are aware of this development.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I would offer that into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 111 shall be assigned Exhibit P2540. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now let's go back to P373B, an intercept from 14 July not to be broadcast. But we can see that it's -- the participants are General Zivanovic, at Zlatar, which you've told us is the code-name for the Drina Corps Command. And Major Jokic, the Palma duty officer. And we can see this, as consistent with your testimony that Jokic was the duty officer that day. And we see that General Zivanovic is passing on information to Jokic but he is saying: Take this as an order. Then -- and says: "Surround the location." How do you interpret General Zivanovic from the Drina Corps Command issuing an order to Major Jokic when we have just seen him being replaced as corps commander the night before?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If I recall, General Krstic's Defence counsel asked me that same question. This is the second of two intercepts related to this particular issue. There's a previous intercept where Obrenovic and the Zvornik Brigade is seeking to find the corps commander. They're unsuccessful in doing that. At some point in this context, General Zivanovic, who is still in Vlasenica at the Drina Corps Command, and who, on the 14th, is now realizing that there is a significant adverse military situation developing at -- or in the zone of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, does reach out through the Zvornik Brigade duty officer and informs him of the situation and what he ought to do. And in this context, he gives an order, as a general. Tells Jokic to tell Obrenovic to take this as an order. It is, perhaps, one of the few orders which, in reality, General Zivanovic might not be authorised to give; but, having said that, he is still a general in the Army of the Republika Srpska. He has recognised a situation that could have a potentially significant adverse impact, and he is taking steps to deal with it. The fact that he does this order in this context is -- is somewhat extraordinary, but, as a general who has an awareness of what's going on and who knows all of the people involved, he -- he gives that order, and for all anybody knows because I don't think we've ever been able to confirm or deny this one way or another, he could even be passing on the order of General Krstic. So it is an outlier in the context of the normal course of how orders are given and why. Obrenovic obviously is engaged in this and takes this as an order, as it's passed down. But I don't -- for the context that we've discussed before, this doesn't offset the fact that on the 14th of July General Krstic is not the corps commander and General Zivanovic has somehow reassumed command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you very briefly tell us what is this emergency that has got General Zivanovic involved in issuing an order. Just very briefly. I think you have referred to it already, but ...

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As I've discussed, the -- during the -- primarily the evening of the 12th and through the day of the 13th, the Zvornik Infantry Brigade as well as the MUP units in and around Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, as reflected by Dragomir Vasic's reports, and Borovcanin's, recognise that the armed head of the column could number as high as 3.000 to 4.000 soldiers. Other evidence that I've discussed reflects the fact that the senior levels of the Drina command on those days believe those numbers are wildly exaggerated, that the military threat is nowhere as significant as Obrenovic has been stating it has been. What this particular intercept and the response of General Zivanovic is, is a recognition that Obrenovic has in fact been very accurate with his estimates of the size of the column and consequently the military threat that it poses to not only the Zvornik Infantry Brigade by the actual town of Zvornik. So at this point in time, you begin to see a series of intercepts reflecting how that knowledge of the military situation being worse than everybody anticipated in Zvornik being passed around and the measures that various command-level elements to include the Drina Corps will be taking over the subsequent hours to combat that threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's go a little later in the evening to 2102 hours. It is P16A. It's the next document in the tab. This is 14 July from the other intercept records in the case in evidence. And we see that it's between Palma duty officer, Major Jokic, and Badem, X and Y, and we see early on someone is asking to talk to Beara. Badem again is who, or what?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Badem is the telephonic code-name for the Bratunac Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we see this. I won't read it all out. The Palma duty officer who we know is Jokic wants -- says: "Beara is needed urgently. Somebody needs him. The higher house urgently needs him ..." And then it says: "But he has to call me." Then as we look down the intercept, we see that Jokic and BE actually start speaking to each other and that Jokic says: "We were together, Colonel, sir, number 155 called you and asked you to call him urgently." So can you tell from this where Jokic is calling from and where he is calling to, looking for Beara?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jokic is calling from his duty location, which is the Zvornik Brigade, where he is the duty officer that day, and he's calling, if he's calling through Badem, he is calling to the Bratunac Infantry Brigade, where he finds Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the "higher house"? What do you think that is a reference to? It's mentioned I see at least twice in this intercept.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on whose reference -- I mean, in the case of Palma, the higher house or the next level of command would be the Drina Corps. In the case of Beara, it would be the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, this line in the middle that says -- where Jokic says: "Number 155, that's, I mean, the higher house, you go ahead and call them, you have, so I don't speak like this." What's Jokic says?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, again, putting it in context of how he is speaking, Jokic, like most other officers, are aware that their telephonic conversations can be monitored by the enemy. So he is attempting to speak cryptically. But he is, as we know, 155 is the number for the Main Staff operations centre. So what he is trying to do in this context is relay to Colonel Beara that he needs to call back to the Main Staff operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then Beara says something, or BE says something according to this that we only have ... for. And Jokic says: "Yes. A: "We have huge problems over here." Then BE, we can't hear anything from BE, or they couldn't. And then Jokic says: "There are big problems, well, with the people -- I mean, with the parcel." And he goes on to say Drago is nowhere around and then he reiterates to call the higher house, 155. What does your analysis reveal Jokic is referring to when he says "We have huge problems, big problems, well, with the people -- I mean, the parcel"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As is evident in other intercepts, parcels was what they would euphemistically call people or, in this particular context, prisoners. Again, not wanting to mention the phrase prisoners over a potentially unsecure line that could be intercepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
